timecoded_text_to_speech.text: My girlfriend, her name is Wanda and you know the actress, Diane Carroll.
She was in Toronto, I think about two or three years ago, maybe two years ago and she
did some set boulevard.
There was this story, Diane came to hear me in a concert in New York and my girlfriend
Wanda was sitting next to her.
So Wanda was telling me this later, she said I was sitting with something and Diane started
crying.
I wanted to see Wanda sitting next to me and say, oh, she's special, she's careless.
You know, you know, dabbing it to her and then Wanda said before long, she had to borrow
her handkerchief and she had to join her.
I don't remember what I was saying but I think it's very special and I think that's one
of the great things about audiences coming to live performances.
There is something, CDs are wonderful, television performances are wonderful, there is still
nothing quite like coming to Roy Thompson Hall, hearing a great orchestra, the Toronto Symphony
Orchestra, their music dreaded and to hear solos who come, you know, to hear a live concert,
there is just nothing like it.
Is that what makes me really sick?
Is the life the same?
It's excellent.
Because you do very well with your life.
I think there's nothing like the live performance.
I think it is probably the most nurturing, the most stimulating.
I love, I have to tell you, the rehearsal process, I love the preparation.
I think I probably even, and even more stimulated in making it happen in rehearsal or even in
my practice situation at home with a piano because you really delve and you're really
taking risks.
You can do it without a safety net because you're at home, nobody hears you if you crack
or you run out of breath or you say the wrong words in particular time but it's exhilarating.
And to be able then to have hopefully gotten all the cobwebs out and then to be in front
of a live audience and to be able to give this live performing experience, I think it's
probably the best part of all.
I love recording and I love, but I think the live performing for me is what makes it.
And, you know, the experience you share just now, when people come backstage, I don't
know what kind of a day someone has or what kind of a week or what kind of a year.
The gentleman in my last performance introduced me to his fiance.
He was middle-aged and it wasn't his first marriage and he was so happy to be starting on
his new life with his wife.
And then he shared with me that he had very, very, very serious cancer.
And what coming to the concert meant to him to be there.
And that's what I mean by life performance.
It's so nurturing, it's healing, it's exciting, it's challenging, it's live music, live
theater.

youtube_description:
Kathleen Battle shares thoughts on what makes live performancs special and the rehearsal process.

(BTW Kathleen Battle doesn't end her sentence "Live music, Live theatre..." because the interviewer interjects a "but" and then asks about how she "exert[s] quality control...")

NOTE: This video is intended for research and educational purposes -- particularly for those interested in singing and/or singing Opera. It is excerpted from a 1999 CBC Interview.
